opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest gap right now isn't raw intelligence on any single task. If you look at individual capabilities, models can already write code, do research, draft documents at a level that's genuinely useful. What's missing is the stuff that makes a human employee reliable over weeks and months, not just over one conversation.

The first thing is long-horizon consistency. A good employee holds context about a project for a long time. They remember why a decision was made three weeks ago, they notice when something drifts from the original goal. Current agent systems still lose the thread. Context windows have gotten bigger, memory mechanisms exist, but the agent doesn't really *own* the task in the way a person does. It's more like a very capable contractor who shows up fresh every morning.

The second thing is coordination. In multi-agent setups, people often imagine you just split work across agents and it scales, like an organization. But organizations work because of a lot of implicit structure: shared norms, knowing who to ask, knowing when to escalate, trusting a colleague's output without re-checking everything. Agents today are not good at calibrating trust in each other. Either they blindly accept another agent's output and errors compound, or you add so much verification that you lose the efficiency gains. Finding that middle ground is still largely unsolved.

Third, and maybe most important, is judgment about when to stop and ask. A good employee knows the boundaries of their authority. They know which decisions they can make alone and which ones need a manager's sign-off. Agents are often either too timid, asking for confirmation on trivial things, or too aggressive, taking irreversible actions without checking. That calibration is really about understanding the human's intent and the stakes of the situation, and it's hard to learn from static training data.

And finally, there's the feedback loop. Human employees get better at a specific job by doing it, getting corrected, and adapting. Most agent systems today don't really learn on the job in a durable way. Each deployment is somewhat frozen. So I think the next big step is some form of continual learning or experience accumulation, where the agent actually improves from working inside a particular team, with its particular way of doing things.

So to summarize, I'd say we've largely solved the "can it do the task" question. What we haven't solved is "can it be trusted to do the job," and that's a different and harder problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability and coordination but does not identify lower cost than hiring a human employee as an adoption condition.

r002.rationale: The response says current systems can perform useful tasks but are not yet trustworthy employees; it does not convey that they have not raised the ceiling of what can ultimately be achieved.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the gap isn't mainly about intelligence anymore. If you look at what a single agent can do today on a well-defined task, it's already quite impressive. The problem shows up the moment you ask many of them to work together over a long horizon, the way a real team does. There are a few things I keep running into.

The first is memory, and I mean memory in a working sense, not just a longer context window. A good employee remembers what we decided last Tuesday, why we decided it, and what we tried that didn't work. Right now most agents start every task close to zero. They can retrieve documents, but retrieval isn't the same as having lived through the project. So they repeat mistakes, they re-derive things, and they don't accumulate the kind of tacit knowledge that makes a senior person valuable.

The second is coordination. When you put several agents together, the failure mode is almost never that one agent is too dumb. It's that they don't know what each other knows. They duplicate work, they hand off tasks with missing context, and errors compound silently along the chain. Humans solve this with a lot of cheap, informal communication, a quick message asking if someone already handled something. Agents today tend to either over-communicate everything or communicate nothing, and neither works. We also don't have good protocols for an agent to say "I'm not confident, someone should check this," which is one of the most important things a junior employee learns to do.

The third, and this is the one I think is underrated, is self-evolution. An employee gets better month over month from feedback. Most multi-agent systems are frozen at deployment. Whatever the planner does on day one is what it does on day two hundred. Until the system can take outcomes, figure out which agent or which step was responsible, and actually improve that part, you're not really hiring an employee. You're renting a very capable contractor who has amnesia every morning.

And then there's reliability over long horizons. A task that needs a hundred steps, each at ninety-nine percent, still fails a third of the time. Real work is full of these long chains. So the system needs recovery, checkpoints, the ability to notice it has drifted and come back, rather than just forward execution and hope.

If I had to summarize, I'd say we have the raw capability but not the organizational layer. Memory, communication, credit assignment, and the ability to learn from your own history. Those are what turn a group of smart individuals into a team, and that's exactly the part we haven't solved yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses memory, coordination, self-evolution, and reliability, but does not identify lower cost than hiring a human employee as an adoption condition.

r002.rationale: The response says current systems have raw capability but lack an organizational layer; it does not convey that they have not raised the ceiling of what can ultimately be achieved.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s still missing is the ability to take responsibility for an outcome over a long period of time. Today, you can give a multi-agent system a fairly clear task, divide it into smaller tasks, and get an impressive result. But an employee has to do more than that. They need to notice when the goal is ambiguous, find the missing context, and recognize when they’re heading in the wrong direction.

Adding more agents doesn’t automatically solve those problems. If they share the same blind spot, they can reinforce one another’s mistakes. So the important question is how they verify work, handle disagreement, and maintain a shared understanding as the task changes.

I’d also emphasize knowing when to ask a human. An effective employee doesn’t ask for permission at every step, but they also don’t confidently make decisions outside their authority. Getting that balance right—working independently while making uncertainty and progress visible—is a big part of moving from an impressive demo to a system you can actually delegate work to.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses what multi-agent systems need to become effective employees, but does not mention their cost relative to hiring a human employee.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes current systems’ shortcomings in handling long-term work, uncertainty, and oversight. It does not say they have failed to raise the ceiling of what can ultimately be achieved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest gap is the ability to take responsibility for an outcome over time. Today, a multi-agent system can divide a task, exchange messages, and produce something that looks convincing. But an effective employee also needs to understand what success means, notice when the work is going off track, and follow through until the result is actually useful.

That requires reliable memory, clear ownership, and the ability to verify work. If several agents collaborate, who checks that their assumptions are consistent? Who resolves disagreements? And when something fails, can the system identify the cause and recover, or does it simply generate another answer?

It also needs judgment about when to act independently and when to ask a person. Asking about every detail creates more management work; silently making consequential assumptions creates risk. Until systems can navigate that balance reliably, people will still spend a lot of effort supervising them. The goal should be less supervision per completed task, rather than simply more agents.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reducing supervision, but does not say multi-agent systems must cost less than hiring a human employee.

r002.rationale: The response describes current gaps in responsibility and follow-through, but does not state that these systems have not raised the ceiling of what can ultimately be achieved.
